paras: The West Fourteenth Street longshoremen's strike riot was a fight on the evening of August 16, 1920, in which striking white longshoremen attacked a group of Black strikebreakers near Fourteenth Street and Ninth Avenue in Manhattan, New York City. Two strikers were shot and several Black workers were injured, and police reserves dispersed the crowds before any arrests were made. New York dailies, a wire dispatch and the Black press reported it, several of them calling it a "race riot."

Coastwise longshoremen in New York had been on strike since March, and the Morgan Steamship line employed Black non-union men on its Piers 13 and 14 on the North River. According to the Sun, police had escorted the Black workers to the Ninth Avenue elevated station at Christopher Street since the strike began, and the strikers had demanded their discharge two days earlier as a condition of settling the strike.

The New-York Tribune reported that about twenty-five Black longshoremen were walking toward the elevated station when bricks, stones and bottles fell around them and about thirty-five white men, "all said to be striking port workers," charged. A wire dispatch likewise said that, according to the police, the strikers started throwing rocks and bottles at the non-union men coming from the piers. The Sun gave a different opening: the Black workers bolted from their police escort into West Fourteenth Street, and one of them, seeing the strikers closing in, fired a pistol into the air.

A running fight followed that the Sun said lasted more than half an hour, with stones thrown through windows and fighting with fists, clubs, bottles and barrel staves. Pursued by white men with clubs, some of the Black workers fled to the platform of the Fourteenth Street elevated station, where the Tribune described a panic among waiting passengers. Police reserves from the Charles Street and West Twentieth Street stations arrived and drove the two sides apart.

Two white strikers were shot: Daniel Curran, 18, of Gansevoort Street, in the chest or abdomen, and a man of 129 East 123d Street named as James Kearns or Joseph Kearons, in the right leg. The Tribune named the injured Black men as John Barnes, found unconscious on Ninth Avenue, Benjamin McNeal and Emil Howard, and said their injuries were not serious; the Sun named Daniel Johnson and Joseph Barnes, at Barnes's same address, with head lacerations.

Police said they had not established who fired the shots and attributed the firing to the strikebreakers. The crowd dispersed before arrests could be made, and a strikers' meeting set for that night to vote on returning to work was not held. The Sun reported one man dying in the hospital, but no later report of a death, an arrest or charges appears in the coverage.

The two New York papers framed the same fight differently: the Tribune headlined "Two Shot, Riot Caused by Port Workers' Fight" and dwelt on hysterical women and Black men "waving their dock hooks" on a train, while the Sun put "2 Shot in Dock Strike Battle" on page one, called it a "race riot" and began its account with a Black man's pistol shot. The Pine Bluff Daily Graphic in Arkansas ran the wire version under "Negroes, Whites, in Riots Over Strike."

In the Black press, the Chicago Defender ran a front-page brief headed "Many Hurt in Strike Breakers' Race Riot," counting four "members of the Race" and two white men injured. An Associated Negro Press item, carried by the Black Dispatch on August 27 and the Savannah Tribune on August 28, called it a "near race riot" with two white and three Black men hurt. Neither added names or comment.

Accounts differed on who began the violence: the Tribune and the wire cited police that the strikers threw the first missiles, while the Sun said a Black worker fired first, into the air. Counts of injured Black men ranged from two in the Sun to three in the ANP item and four in the Defender, with the Tribune adding that "many" had minor injuries.

bases: Striking white longshoremen fought Black strikebreakers employed by the Morgan line on their way home from the piers, during a strike in which the strikers had demanded the strikebreakers' discharge (A1, A2, A4).

accounts.label: New-York Tribune / police
accounts.gist: About 25 Black longshoremen walking to the elevated station were showered with bricks, stones and bottles and charged by about 35 white strikers; police attributed the shots that wounded two strikers to the strikebreakers.

accounts.label: The Sun and New York Herald
accounts.gist: The Black workers bolted from their police escort, and one fired a pistol into the air as strikers closed in; both sides then fought along Fourteenth Street for more than half an hour.

accounts.label: Wire report
accounts.gist: Strikers, according to police, began throwing rocks and bottles at non-union men coming from the piers; revolvers were drawn and two strikers were hit.

accounts.label: Black press (Defender, ANP)
accounts.gist: Twenty-five Black strikebreakers for the Morgan line were set upon by striking longshoremen on the way home; four (Defender) or three (ANP) Black men and two white men were injured.

framing.detail: The Tribune headlined 'Two Shot, Riot Caused by Port Workers' Fight' and stressed panic among passengers and 'hysterical' women, with the Black men 'yelling and waving their dock hooks'.
The Sun ran it on page one as '2 Shot in Dock Strike Battle', calling it a 'race riot' and opening the fight with a Black man's pistol shot.
An Arkansas paper ran the wire version under 'Negroes, Whites, in Riots Over Strike', citing police that the strikers started it.
The Defender's front-page brief 'Many Hurt in Strike Breakers' Race Riot' and the ANP's 'near race riot' item gave casualty counts without comment.

versions.value: Strikers threw bricks, stones and bottles at the Black workers and charged them
A Black man who had bolted the police escort fired a pistol into the air as strikers closed in

conflicts.note: The Tribune and the wire both cite police that the strikers began the attack; the Sun's version puts the first shot on a Black worker. The versions may describe different moments of the same fight.
Counts differ by paper; the local Tribune names three Black men and the Sun two, with Barnes common to both.
Each pair shares an address (251 West 61st Street; 129 East 123d Street), so they are probably the same two men.

In another moment about thirty-five white men, all said to be striking port workers, were charging down on the negroes.
The police say the identity of the persons who fired the shots has not been established. The firing is attributed to the strike breakers.
